newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Switzerland's CS takes big charge, sees loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Switzerland's CS takes big charge, sees loss.

text.p: CS Holding emulated its big Swiss banking rivals on Friday announcing a 3.9 billion franc ($2.9 billion) extraordinary charge and saying it would be in the red 1996 following sweeping changes to the way it provides for credit losses.
The financial services group, which in July announced a major restructuring, said it was setting aside the 3.9 billion francs in the form of extraordinary reserves, provisions and depreciation.
As a result, it expected a 1996 consolidated loss before deduction of minority interests of around 2.1 billion francs compared with a 1995 profit of 1.54 billion.
Despite the expected 1996 loss, CS Holding will maintain its the dividend at the 1995 level of four francs per share.
CS said its new credit risk management method constituted a shift away from provisioning for actual defaults to a system of setting provisions for statistically expected credit losses.
The move follows a similar step taken by rival Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) in September. SBC was the first Swiss bank to adopt such a method of calculating loss provisions.
Swiss banks have all been suffering from high loan-loss provisions and credit losses in their domestic business as a result of the sharp and lasting downturn in the Swiss economy.
Analysts had expected the CS Holding move in view of the dire bad loan situation in the domestic sector.
"A cleaning out is something I always wanted to see," said James Hyde at Merrill Lynch in London.

"If they hadn't done anything this year, the comparisons next year would be bad," said Zuercher Kantonalbank analyst Christof Bieri in referring to comparisons to the two other big banks in Switzerland.
As part of its restructuring, SBC is taking write-offs totalling 3.3 billion francs this year, a step that will result in an estimated 1996 loss of 1.9 billion.

Union Bank of Switzerland, while not revamping its provisioning methods, is taking a three billion franc charge to cover credit risk and domestic restructuring that will result in a 1996 loss of some 500 million francs.
The CS announcement outlining the measures was generally viewed as positive, but some analysts said there were still some unanswered questions.

"It remains to be seen if this (the 3.9 billion) is enough," said Kleinwort Benson analyst James Alexander. He said that before making a final determination, analysts would have to see more details on the group's non-performing loan portfolio.
And while CS Holding, like SBC, is setting up a two billion franc credit risk fluctuation reserve, it gave no information on the level of annual value adjustments, Bieri said.
SBC said in September that it would take annual recurring charges of around 600 million francs starting in 1997. This equals the expected annual loss on the existing loan book.

Separately, CS Holding said a consortium comprising German energy companies Bayernwerk, Badenwerk and Energieversorgung Schwaben (EVS), Swiss utility Nordostschweizerische Kraftwerke (NOK) and CS Holding will take over CS Holding's current stake in newly-formed Watt AG.

Earlier this month Elektrowatt, 44.9 percent owned by CS Holding, said it was spinning off its utility interests into Watt. At that time CS Holding said it was keeping its stake in both Watt and Elektrowatt.
Following today's announcements, Standard & Poor's cut the long-term debt ratings of Credit Suisse and related entities, and Credit Suisse Financial Products to AA from AA plus.
But it raised the long-term debt ratings of CS First Boston Inc to AA from A and the short-term ratings to A1 plus from A1.

The European credit rating agency IBCA left its rating on Credit Suisse Group, the entity that will result from the previously announced restructuring of CS Holding, unchanged at AA. But the Credit Suisse bank unit's rating was cut to AA minus from AAA.
($1=1.3367 Swiss Franc)
